Pilot Sample Size for Two Stage Bounded Risk Estimation of an Exponential Mean

Source: R/ts_br_exp_mean.R
ts_br_exp_mean_pilot.Rd

Returns the first stage (pilot) sample size for the two stage bounded risk point estimation procedure for the mean of an exponential distribution, evaluated by ts_br_exp_mean. The loss in estimating the mean \(\theta\) by the sample mean is \(A\,(\bar{X} - \theta)^2\), and the procedure keeps its expectation, the risk, at or below w.

Usage

ts_br_exp_mean_pilot(A, w, m_0 = 20, gamma = 1)

Arguments

A

The loss constant: the loss is \(A\,(\bar{X} - \theta)^2\). A single positive number, in the units of w per squared unit of the data.

w

The risk bound: the largest acceptable expected loss. A single positive number.

m_0

The smallest first stage sample size to return. A whole number of at least 3. Default 20; see Details.

gamma

Positive tuning constant of the pilot rule. Larger values give a smaller first stage. Default 1, for which the rule is \(\lceil \sqrt{A / w} \rceil\).

Value

A length one integer: the first stage sample size.

Details

The source of the procedure (Mukhopadhyay and de Silva, 2009, Section 8.3.1) requires only that the first stage have at least three observations and gives no rule for choosing its size. The choice does not affect the risk bound, but it decides how many observations the procedure uses. Writing \(n^* = A \theta^2 / w\) for the sample size at which the risk \(A \theta^2 / n\) of a fixed sample equals w, the expected total sample size for a first stage of \(m\) observations is, when \(n^*\) is well above \(m\), $$E[N] / n^* \approx 0.565 \times \frac{2 (m + 1)^2}{(m - 1)(m - 2)},$$ where 0.565 is the constant of Zacks and Mukhopadhyay (2006; the book's Equation 8.3.13) and the rest is the expectation of the stopping variable (Equations 8.3.9 and 8.3.11).

\(m\)351015203050
\(E[N] / n^*\)9.043.391.901.591.461.341.25

The ratio falls toward 1.13 as \(m\) grows. (Exact calculation agrees with the approximation to within 1 percent once \(n^*\) is at least five times \(m\), and to within 6 percent when \(n^*\) is as small as \(m\).) A first stage of three observations therefore uses about nine times the optimal sample size. On the other side, a first stage larger than \(n^*\) is itself the waste: the total can never be smaller than \(m\). The first stage should be as large as one can be confident does not exceed \(n^*\).

The pilot size returned is $$m = \max\{m_0,\ \lceil (A / w)^{1/(1 + \gamma)} \rceil\}.$$ With the default m_0 = 20, a first stage of 20 keeps the expected total within about 1.5 times \(n^*\) whenever \(n^*\) is at least 20 (1.54 at \(n^* = 20\), 1.47 at 50). The second term raises \(A / w\), which is \(n^*\) for \(\theta = 1\), to the power \(1/(1 + \gamma)\), so that the first stage grows with the size of the problem but more slowly than \(n^*\) does. This is the form of pilot that Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2016, Equation 24) recommend, following Mukhopadhyay and de Silva (2009), for a purely sequential procedure. Using it here is this package's choice; as said above, the source of this two stage procedure gives no rule. If the mean is expected to be so small that \(n^* = A \theta^2 / w\) may be below 20, lower m_0.

References

Chattopadhyay, B., & Kelley, K. (2016). Estimation of the coefficient of variation with minimum risk: A sequential method for minimizing sampling error and study cost. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 51(5), 627–648. doi:10.1080/00273171.2016.1203279

Mukhopadhyay, N., & de Silva, B. M. (2009). Sequential methods and their applications. Chapman & Hall/CRC. ISBN:9780367386535

Zacks, S., & Mukhopadhyay, N. (2006). Bounded risk estimation of the exponential parameter in a two-stage sampling. Sequential Analysis, 25(4), 437–452. doi:10.1080/07474940600934896 (As described in Mukhopadhyay and de Silva, 2009, Section 8.3.2, Equation 8.3.13.)

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu, Bhargab Chattopadhyay bhargab@iiitvadodara.ac.in

Examples

# Mean time between service calls, squared error loss with A = 100,
# risk at most 4.
ts_br_exp_mean_pilot(A = 100, w = 4)
#> [1] 20

# A demanding bound: the rule exceeds the minimum.
ts_br_exp_mean_pilot(A = 100, w = 0.01)
#> [1] 100

# A smaller first stage, accepted knowingly (see the table in Details).
ts_br_exp_mean_pilot(A = 100, w = 4, m_0 = 10)
#> [1] 10
